title: Houthi Strike Damages Top Floors of Aramco Headquarters in Dhahran
excerpt: The strike hit the executive tower of the world’s largest oil company, damaging the chief executive’s floor with no casualties; Brent crude settled above $106.
body:
• A Houthi strike damaged the top three floors of Saudi Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran on Tuesday night, including the chief executive's offices; there were no casualties at the building, officials told AP.
  • Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry described a "limited fire" at the administrative building; Aramco did not immediately comment.
  • The Houthis claimed a multi-target operation against Aramco in Dhahran, King Khalid airport and a Riyadh refinery; the refinery claim is not independently verified.
  • Oil rose on the news: Brent settled Wednesday at $106.06 a barrel and WTI at $95.09, a three-week high.

A Houthi strike has damaged the top three floors of Saudi Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran, including the offices of the chief executive and other senior officials, two regional officials told the Associated Press. There were no casualties at the headquarters building. Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry reported a "limited fire" at the administrative building on Tuesday night; Aramco did not immediately respond to AP's request for comment.

The strike marks an escalation in target selection: after a week of attacks on Saudi airports, the Houthis have now hit the executive tower of the world's largest oil company — while leaving its production and export infrastructure, on current reporting, untouched.

Claims and Interceptions

The Houthis had warned earlier that they were targeting Dhahran with a ballistic missile. On Wednesday, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree claimed a multi-target operation spanning Aramco in Dhahran, King Khalid airport and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh, using ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones; the refinery element is a Houthi claim that AP did not verify. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two drones, four cruise missiles and one ballistic missile targeting Riyadh, a ballistic missile targeting Dhahran and a cruise missile targeting Al-Kharj; debris from an intercepted strike over Riyadh injured one person on Wednesday.

The Houthis framed the attacks as retaliation for Saudi operations against Sanaa and other areas. A senior Houthi official told AP that Oman had tried to reopen negotiations, and Russia and China had tried via Iran, and that the group welcomes mediation toward a comprehensive end to the war.

Markets and the Wider War

Oil markets took the strike seriously but not catastrophically: Brent crude settled Wednesday at $106.06 a barrel and US WTI at $95.09, a three-week high, in figures reported by Reuters and the Wall Street Journal. The reaction was muted compared with the 2019 Abqaiq attack because the damage was to an administrative tower, not processing or export capacity, and no production disruption has been reported.

The harder problem is arithmetic. Regional officials say Saudi Arabia is running low on interceptors after a week in which, by Cirium's count, more than 3,000 Saudi flights were cancelled or not operated, and AP reports President Trump is evaluating whether the United States should join Saudi strikes. It is in that context that India's embassy in Riyadh told Indians in the kingdom on Thursday to stay indoors during aerial attacks — the community living under this air war numbers roughly 2.4–2.7 million people.
